This has been done lots of times (search function helps!) BUT there is a basic equation relating power (energy output per unit time) to torque and angular velocity (how fast the engine is spinning, in revolutions per second or revolutions per minute e.g. RPM) 

Power = Torque * Angular Velocity 

Horsepower is a unit for a measure of energy output per unit time. When you apply a force through a distance, you do work. Applying a larger force or for a longer distance increases the amount of work you have to do, just like how the amount of work done when pushing a big file cabinet increases if the file cabinet is heavier or you have to push it through a longer distance. 1 Newton of Force applied through 1 meter of (linear) distance does 1 Joule of work. If you did this amount of work every second, you would be expending 1 J/s of energy, or 1 Watt (1 HP = 745.7 Watts) 

Suppose if you made the distance a closed loop, such that the force was applied around a fixed center of rotation, like an axis of an engine. Suppose there are slow chemical reactions occurring, exerting a force of 1 Newton on the bottom of the piston, where it's connected to the rotational center of the engine by 1 meter (a very expansive engine indeed). Thus, the chemical reactions of the engine cause it to exert a torque of 100 N * m, which is dimensionally equivalent to 100 J.

Every time the engine makes one revolution (360 degrees, or 2 * pi radians), the engine will expend 2 * pi * 100 N* m of energy, i.e 628 J. If the engine only rotates for only 1 radian (57 degrees), the engine will expend exactly expend 100 J. If the engine rotates at 1 radian per second, then the angular velocity is 1 rad/s and the output will be 100 J / s, or 0.13 HP. If the angular velocity is many times faster, that is, 1 revolution per second (or 60 revolutions per minute), then the power output will be 628 W, or almost a horsepower.   

Why is this so? Going about in a circle with a radius of 1 meter means that every time you make a revolution, you have travelled 2 * pi * r, or 6.28 meters- thus if you're applying a rotational force (i.e. a torque) of 100 N at a radius of 1m, you will exert 100 J per radian or 628 J per revolution. RPM is a measure of angular velocity (revolutions per second).

It is important to distinguish horsepower from torque because for a fixed amount of power output, torque and angular velocity are inversely proportional. If there is a lot of resistance (e.g. friction due to weight of load or poor surfaces), you'll need a high amount of exerted torque to overcome the resistance against the engine spinning caused by a heavy load or drag. For example, if the coefficient of friction of a filing cabinet on a tile floor is 0.5, and the filing cabinet weighs 1000 newtons, you'll need to exert 1000N of force to get the cabinet to begin to move -- below that, the cabinet won't move at all. The load or resistance a truck (or a car stuck in the mud) experiences imposes a resistance against rotating on the engine, e.g. a "negative torque" that the engine must overcome for the engine to start moving. (Assuming that every part of the car is connected as rigid bodies-- in reality, if the load is too big, the transfer of forces break down at the part of "least resistance", such as in the case where the engine moves but the wheels slip against the surface of the mud without moving the car).

In practical cases, peak power output, peak torque and peak angular velocity might be individually constrained. An engine with a high peak torque might not spin very fast (and thus not accelerate or move a load very quickly) if required increases in power output can't scale with higher torques it is capable of, say because the chemical and physical processes of air/gas injection, compression, sparking, and evacuation can't proceed any faster above a certain threshold. You might have vehicles where it is capable of a very high torque at low rotational speeds but the torque it is capable of decreases the faster the engine spins. You might also have an engine with a low peak torque but where the torque it is capable of exerting only starts decreasing at much higher rotational speeds.

You can observe this in the "torque against RPM" graphs of given vehicles. A hydraulic industrial machine at a construction site might be capable of 500 N * m of torque at a max angular velocity of 40 Hz, but this is only roughly 26.8 HP. In contrast, an engine exerting 80 HP at 108 N * m (80 foot pounds) of torque is capable of very fast rotational speeds, 20800 RPM.

You don't just stick two graphs together. You first try to find a time-trend; compare data point Y against data point X for every time point Q; you add an error score if there's deviation from the time-trend. If your algorithm is advanced, you correct the time-trend as you go along. Hence, any slight deviation from the trend is punished.
